start_here.title: How a web app fits together
start_here.summary: Every web app is the same few pieces talking to each other. Know what each piece does and where your secrets live, and most choices get easier.

layers.name: Browser
layers.plain: The screens people see and click. It runs on their device.
layers.rule: Everything sent to the browser is public. Anyone can open the developer tools and read it.

layers.name: Server
layers.plain: Your private code. It checks who someone is, reads the database and calls paid services.
layers.rule: Secrets and anything that costs money belong here, never in browser code.

layers.name: Database
layers.plain: Where your app remembers things between visits: accounts, posts, orders.
layers.rule: Decide who may read each row, or anyone who finds the address can.

layers.name: Outside services
layers.plain: Other companies' tools you call over the internet: payments, email, AI, maps.
layers.rule: Each one adds a key to protect, a bill to watch and something that can go down.

layers.name: Environment variables
layers.plain: Settings and keys handed to your app from outside its code, different on your laptop and in production.
layers.rule: Keep them out of your code and out of git. Put them in your host's settings instead.

framework.what: The toolkit your app's code is written in. It gives pages, routing and server code a shared structure.
framework.why: It is the foundation every other part plugs into, so it limits which hosts and services fit well.
choosing: Does it have server code? You need it for secret keys, payments and AI calls.
Is it in a language you know or want to learn?
Does your host support it fully, without extra setup?
Could you move it to another host later?
watch_for: Picking a browser-only framework, then needing somewhere safe for a payment or AI key.
Choosing by popularity without checking your host supports it.

hosting.what: The computers that run your app all day and give it a public address.
hosting.why: Your laptop sleeps. A host keeps the app up for everyone, all the time.
choosing: How code runs: serverless, an always-on server, or the edge. This changes speed, cost and what works.
Does it offer a persistent disk, background workers or scheduled jobs, if you need them?
Does it fully support your framework?
Does the free plan allow a commercial app?
watch_for: Expecting work to keep running after a serverless request ends. It usually stops.
Building live chat on a host that can't hold connections open.

domain.what: Your app's own address, like yourapp.com, instead of the free one your host gives you.
domain.why: People trust and remember a real name, and email services need a verified domain to send as you.
choosing: The renewal price, not just the discounted first year.
Is WHOIS privacy free?
Can you manage DNS records in the same account for free?
How easy is it to transfer out later?
watch_for: Buying a domain and never adding the DNS records your host and email service ask for.
Budgeting for the first-year price and getting surprised at renewal.
Assuming owning the domain lets you send email from it. You still verify it with the email service.

read_more.title: What happens when you update your DNS?

database.what: Where your app keeps anything it must remember: accounts, posts, bookings.
database.why: Without one, everything disappears when the page reloads.
choosing: Relational (tables) or document (JSON-like)? Relational suits most apps.
Does it work from serverless code, or does it need connection pooling?
Can it push live updates, if your app needs them?
Does it have a mobile SDK, if a phone app may come later?
watch_for: Saving data to a file on a host with no persistent disk. It vanishes on the next deploy.
Leaving tables readable by anyone because access rules felt like extra work.
Running out of connections once real traffic arrives on serverless hosting.

login.what: How people create an account, sign in and stay signed in.
login.why: Once someone sees their own data, your app must know who is asking.
choosing: Ready-made sign-in screens, or build your own?
Sign in with Google or GitHub (OAuth), and email links (magic links)?
A mobile SDK, if a phone app may come later?
Does your database know who is logged in, so its access rules work?
watch_for: Writing your own password storage. Use a login service instead.
Picking login and database separately, then finding they don't share who is logged in.
Checking permissions only in the browser. The server or database must check too.

files.what: Where uploads live: photos, videos, PDFs. Kept apart from the database, which is built for rows, not large files.
files.why: Uploads need a durable home and a way to serve them only to the people allowed to see them.
choosing: Can browsers upload straight to storage with a signed URL?
Does it charge for downloads (egress), not just storage?
Are files served through a CDN?
How do you keep private files private?
watch_for: Sending big uploads through your own server, where size and time limits cut them off.
Making every file public because private access felt like extra work.
Trusting a file's name or type as sent by the browser.

read_more.title: Upload and download with presigned URLs

payments.what: How your app charges people, once or on a subscription, and knows what they paid for.
payments.why: Handling card numbers yourself is risky and regulated. A provider takes that on and tells your app when a payment succeeds.
choosing: Is it a merchant of record? That decides who handles sales tax and VAT.
Does it support subscriptions?
What does each sale cost in fees?
How hard would switching be later?
watch_for: Putting the secret key in browser code.
Unlocking access on the checkout redirect instead of the webhook. Redirects get skipped; webhooks arrive.
Not verifying webhook signatures, so anyone can fake a payment.

read_more.title: Receive events in your webhook endpoint
What is a merchant of record?

ai.what: The AI model provider your app calls to answer, summarize, extract or generate.
ai.why: You get AI features through an API without training a model yourself.
choosing: Is there a free tier or credits for building?
A range of models, so simple tasks use a cheaper, faster one?
An SDK for your server's language?
Clear rate limits, and a way to handle hitting them?
watch_for: Calling the provider from browser code, which exposes your key.
Using the biggest model for every request.
Trusting text from users or web pages as instructions. That is prompt injection.

scraping.what: A tool that fetches other websites and turns them into data your app can use.
scraping.why: Sites are built for people, not programs. A scraper loads the page, often runs its JavaScript, and hands back the content.
choosing: Does it run JavaScript? Many sites are empty without it.
Does it return clean text or Markdown ready for an AI model?
Hosted service, or run it yourself?
What do JavaScript-heavy pages cost?
watch_for: Ignoring robots.txt or a site's terms. Check both before you build on a site.
Collecting personal data with no reason and no plan to protect it.
Sending requests so fast you look like an attack. Slow down and back off.

jobs.what: Work your app does outside a page request: resizing images, sending batches of email, nightly cleanup.
jobs.why: Slow work shouldn't make people wait, and timed work needs to run with nobody clicking.
choosing: Can jobs run on a schedule (cron)?
Do failed jobs retry from a queue instead of vanishing?
Can your host run background workers at all?
Can you see whether each job succeeded?
watch_for: Doing slow work inside a web request, where a time limit cuts it off halfway.
Jobs that do damage when retried, like charging twice. Make each job safe to run again.
No alerts, so a failing job goes unnoticed for weeks.

email.what: How your app sends messages on its own: welcome emails, password resets, receipts.
email.why: Some things only work through an inbox. A personal email account isn't built to send them reliably.
choosing: Built for transactional email, not bulk marketing?
SMTP, an API, or both?
How much DNS setup before the first send?
Will it tell you about bounces and spam complaints?
watch_for: Sending from an unverified domain, so mail lands in spam or bounces.
Sending app email from a personal inbox.
Mixing marketing and password resets on one address, so spam complaints block both.

analytics.what: Counts visitors and shows what they do: pages viewed, where they came from, what they click.
analytics.why: It replaces guesses with numbers: are people finding the app, and where do they give up?
choosing: Does it use cookies? That decides whether you need a consent banner.
Can it track events like sign-ups, not just page views?
Is the free plan permanent or a trial?
Can you export your data if you switch?
watch_for: Setting analytics cookies before visitors agree. EU and UK rules require consent first.
Sending names or emails as event data.
Treating a free trial as a free plan.

monitoring.what: Catches errors real people hit and tells you what broke, on which line, and what they did first.
monitoring.why: Most bugs happen on devices you'll never see. Without monitoring, you hear about them only if someone emails you.
choosing: Does the free error allowance fit your app?
Does it show what the person did before the error?
Does it also check the app is up at all?
How much can your AI builder set up for you?
watch_for: Installing it only in the browser and missing server errors.
Not uploading source maps, so every error points at minified code.
Turning on session replay without masking personal data.

mobile.what: Whether your app could also ship as a phone app in the App Store or Google Play.
mobile.why: Phone apps are built differently, and not every login or database service works from one.
choosing: Do your login and database have phone SDKs, not just web ones?
React Native (shares patterns with web code) or fully native?
What do store rules say about your payments?
Does sign-in with Google or Apple work inside the app?
watch_for: Picking a login or database with no mobile SDK, then rebuilding it for the phone app.
Assuming a phone app is the website in a wrapper. Store review can require real changes, especially for payments.

automations.what: A service that runs workflows between your app and other tools, like posting to Slack when someone books.
automations.why: It already knows hundreds of tools, so a workflow takes minutes instead of a day of code.
choosing: Priced per task, per run, or free when self-hosted?
Can your app start a workflow with a webhook, and can a workflow call your app back?
Can a step run your own code?
Can you self-host it, if data must stay on your servers?
watch_for: Per-step pricing that makes a busy workflow expensive.
Core business logic hidden in workflows nobody can find later.

data_apis.what: Information your app reads from another company's service: scores, weather, maps, prices.
data_apis.why: You can show data you don't own, but the provider sets the rules: keys, limits and how stable it is.
choosing: Official and documented, or unofficial and likely to break?
Does it need a key? Keep it on your server.
How often can you call it, and what happens past the limit?
What does your app show when it's slow or down?
watch_for: Calling it on every page view instead of caching the answer.
Treating an unofficial API as if it came with a promise.

serverless.plain: Your code runs only when a request arrives, on machines the host manages. Nothing sits running between requests.
serverless.matters: Cheap when idle, but long tasks and open database connections are harder.

server.plain: A computer running your app's private code: the part that reads the database, checks passwords and calls paid APIs.
server.matters: Secrets must live here. Put them in browser code and anyone can read them.

cold-start.plain: The delay when serverless code runs after sitting idle, while the host starts a fresh copy.
cold-start.matters: The first visit after a quiet spell can feel slow.

edge.plain: Code that runs on servers spread around the world, close to each visitor.
edge.matters: Faster for a global audience, but edge runtimes support fewer features than a full server.

persistent-disk.plain: Storage attached to a server that survives restarts and deploys.
persistent-disk.matters: Without one, anything your app writes to a file disappears on the next deploy.

environment-variable.plain: A setting passed to your app from outside its code, with different values on your laptop and in production.
environment-variable.matters: Keys and passwords go here, never in code or git.

api-key.plain: A password-like string that identifies your app to another service and decides who gets billed.
api-key.matters: Whoever has it can act as your app and run up your bill.

secret-key.plain: An API key that must stay on your server. Often paired with a publishable key that is safe to share.
secret-key.matters: A leaked secret key can move money or spend credits. Keep it in an environment variable.

read_more.title: Best practices for managing secret API keys

publishable-key.plain: The public half of a key pair. Safe in browser code because it can only start actions, not complete them.
publishable-key.matters: Knowing which key is which stops you exposing the wrong one.

webhook.plain: A message another service sends to your server when something happens, like a payment succeeding.
webhook.matters: Unlocking what someone paid for usually depends on handling this message correctly.

relational-database.plain: Stores data in linked tables of rows and columns, like connected spreadsheets. Postgres and MySQL are examples.
relational-database.matters: A good default. The database itself enforces rules, like every order having a real customer.

document-database.plain: Stores each record as a flexible, JSON-like document. Records don't need the same fields.
document-database.matters: Forgiving while your data's shape changes, but relationships take more work.

row-level-security.plain: Rules inside the database that decide, row by row, who can read or change data.
row-level-security.matters: Protects data even when your app's own checks have a bug.

connection-pooling.plain: Sharing a small set of open database connections across many requests.
connection-pooling.matters: Serverless code can open hundreds of connections at once. Pooling keeps you under the database's limit.

realtime.plain: Changes pushed to everyone watching the moment they happen, with no refresh.
realtime.matters: Without it built in, live updates need an extra service.

websocket.plain: A connection the browser and server keep open so either side can send at any time.
websocket.matters: Chat and multiplayer need a host that can hold these open.

egress.plain: Data leaving a service, usually people downloading files.
egress.matters: Cheap storage can still cost a lot if many people download the files.

cdn.plain: A content delivery network: servers worldwide that keep copies of your files near visitors.
cdn.matters: Images and files load faster for people far from your main server.

merchant-of-record.plain: The company that is legally the seller. It calculates, collects and pays sales tax and VAT for you.
merchant-of-record.matters: Without one, tax in every country you sell to is your job.

read_more.title: What is a merchant of record?

sales-tax.plain: Tax added to a sale (VAT outside the US). The rate depends on where the buyer is, not where you are.
sales-tax.matters: Unless your provider is a merchant of record, you calculate, collect and file it.

subscription.plain: A charge that repeats on a schedule until cancelled.
subscription.matters: Needs a provider that retries failed renewals and handles cancellations.

free-tier.plain: A no-cost plan with usage limits.
free-tier.matters: Good for building and testing. Check what you pay once you pass the limits.

rate-limit.plain: A cap on how many requests you can make in a time window. Extra requests are rejected.
rate-limit.matters: Your app must wait and retry, not crash, when it hits one.

token.plain: A small chunk of text, often part of a word, that AI models read and write. Usage is priced in tokens.
token.matters: Input and output both count, so long prompts and documents cost more.

model.plain: The specific AI system a request goes to. Providers offer several, trading speed and cost against capability.
model.matters: Using a bigger model than the task needs is the easiest way to overspend.

cron.plain: A schedule for running code automatically, like every night at midnight. Named after an old Unix tool.
cron.matters: Anything that runs on a timer, like a daily digest, needs it.

background-job.plain: Work done outside a page request, so nobody waits on it.
background-job.matters: Slow work belongs here, not in the request that loads a page.

queue.plain: A waiting line of jobs, handled in order, retried if they fail.
queue.matters: A job that fails partway is still there to try again, not lost.

transactional-email.plain: Email sent because one person did something: a password reset, a receipt, a sign-up code.
transactional-email.matters: People are waiting for it, so it must arrive fast and not land in spam.

smtp.plain: The standard protocol mail servers use to hand email to each other.
smtp.matters: The universal fallback when a service's own API doesn't fit your setup.

domain-verification.plain: Proving you control a domain, usually by adding DNS records (SPF, DKIM) the service gives you.
domain-verification.matters: Without it, your email lands in spam or is refused.

sdk.plain: A software development kit: a provider's ready-made code for using their service from your app.
sdk.matters: One for your platform, web or phone, saves you writing and maintaining that code.

react-native.plain: A framework for building iPhone and Android apps with React, the same patterns many web apps use.
react-native.matters: Lets skills and some logic carry over from a website to a phone app.

app-store.plain: Apple's App Store or Google Play. Both review every app, including how it takes payments and handles data.
app-store.matters: Shipping a phone app means planning for review, not just finishing the code.

oauth.plain: Signing in with an account from elsewhere, like Google, without your app ever seeing that password.
oauth.matters: A button is faster than a form, and there is no new password to forget.

magic-link.plain: A one-time sign-in link sent by email. Clicking it signs you in, no password.
magic-link.matters: No passwords means none to reuse or steal.

signed-url.plain: A temporary link to a private file, carrying proof it was approved. It expires.
signed-url.matters: Browsers upload and download private files directly, without passing every byte through your server.

read_more.title: Upload and download with presigned URLs

portability.plain: How easily you could swap one part for another later. Standard tools move easily; provider-only features don't.
portability.matters: Rarely urgent at launch. It matters when a price changes or you outgrow a plan.

vendor-lock-in.plain: How stuck you are with one provider. Leaving would mean rewriting code, not changing a setting.
vendor-lock-in.matters: Often a fair trade for speed. Know where you have it.

registrar.plain: The company you buy and renew a domain from. ICANN accredits them and sets the rules.
registrar.matters: It sets your renewal price, whether privacy and DNS are free, and how easy leaving is.

dns.plain: The internet's address book. Records like A, CNAME and MX point your domain at your host and email service.
dns.matters: A new domain points nowhere until you add the records your host and email service give you.

whois-privacy.plain: Replaces your name, address and phone in the public domain directory with the registrar's details.
whois-privacy.matters: Without it, your home address can be public. Most registrars include it free.

headless-browser.plain: A real browser, like Chrome, running without a window so a program can control it.
headless-browser.matters: Needed for JavaScript-heavy pages, but slower and costlier than a plain fetch.

robots-txt.plain: A file where a site says which pages bots may visit. A request, not a lock.
robots-txt.matters: Ignoring it can get you blocked, and matters more if the site's terms also forbid scraping.

page-view.plain: One load of one page, the most basic thing analytics counts.
page-view.matters: Shows traffic, not what people did. Pair it with events.

event.plain: One action someone takes, like signing up or clicking Buy, tracked on its own.
event.matters: Events tell you whether a feature is used, not just visited.

cookie-consent.plain: A visitor's clear yes before non-essential cookies are set, usually through a banner.
cookie-consent.matters: The EU and UK require it before most analytics cookies, not after.

source-map.plain: A file that maps the compressed code your app runs back to the code you wrote.
source-map.matters: Without it, error reports point at unreadable minified code.

session-replay.plain: A video-like recording of what someone clicked and saw before an error.
session-replay.matters: Shows the bug happening, but records real people. Mask personal data first.

uptime.plain: An outside service requests your app on a timer to see if it answers.
uptime.matters: When the whole app is down it can't report its own error. Only an outside check notices.
